title: Cold War and Decolonization
bigQuestion: How did a world divided between two superpowers also become a world of dozens of new nations, and why did the division end the way it did?

story.title: The Note That Opened a Wall
story.kicker: On the evening of November 9, 1989, an East German official read a piece of paper he had not studied, and by midnight the most famous wall in the world was open.
paragraphs: For twenty-eight years the Berlin Wall had cut a city in half. It went up in August 1961 to stop East Germans from escaping to the West, and it worked: a concrete barrier, a strip of raked sand, guard towers, dogs, and orders to shoot. At least one hundred and forty people died trying to cross it. Families waved to each other across it on holidays. Children grew up never having seen the other side of their own street.

By the fall of 1989, East Germany was in trouble. Hungary had opened its border with Austria, and tens of thousands of East Germans were driving to Hungary and simply walking out. Every Monday, crowds in the city of Leipzig marched through the streets chanting that they were the people. The government, terrified of a bloodbath and without the backing of the Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev, decided to ease travel rules to calm things down. A new regulation was drafted allowing citizens to apply for permits to travel abroad. It was supposed to take effect the next day, with paperwork.

That evening a party spokesman named Günter Schabowski held a televised press conference. Near the end, a reporter asked about travel. Schabowski, who had been handed the note just before the broadcast and had not read it carefully, fumbled through it and announced that East Germans could now cross the border. A reporter asked when. Schabowski looked at the paper, shrugged, and said: as far as I know, immediately, without delay. Television carried it live. Within an hour, West German news was reporting that the wall was open.

Thousands of East Berliners walked to the crossing points and demanded to be let through. The border guards had no orders. They phoned their superiors, who had no orders either. The crowds grew. Around eleven-thirty at night, the commander at the Bornholmer Street crossing, facing a crowd of thousands and fearing a stampede, opened the gate. Other crossings followed. East and West Berliners met on top of the wall, hugging strangers and hammering at the concrete with whatever they had.

No one had planned this. Not the East German government, not Gorbachev, not the Western leaders who watched on television with their mouths open. A system built on fear had run out of people willing to shoot. Within a year Germany was reunited. Within two years the Soviet Union itself was gone. This chapter tells the story of how the world came to be divided by that wall, what happened in the rest of the world while it stood, and why it fell.
story.think: The wall fell because guards without orders chose not to shoot. What had to change, over years, for that moment to be possible?

lessons.title: The Iron Curtain Falls
lessons.mainIdea: Between 1945 and 1949 the wartime alliance broke into two hostile blocs, one led by the United States and one by the Soviet Union, divided by what Churchill called an iron curtain.
reading: In February 1945, with Germany nearly beaten, Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin met at Yalta on the Black Sea. They agreed to divide Germany into occupation zones and promised free elections in the countries the Red Army had liberated. Stalin had a different idea of free. Within two years, communist parties backed by Soviet troops and secret police had taken over Poland, Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria. Opposition leaders were jailed or killed. In March 1946 Winston Churchill, speaking in Fulton, Missouri, said that an *iron curtain* had come down across Europe from the Baltic Sea to the Adriatic. The phrase stuck.

Each side saw the other as the aggressor. To Americans, Stalin was swallowing Eastern Europe and would take the rest if he could. To Stalin, whose country had been invaded from the west twice in thirty years and had lost twenty-seven million people, a ring of friendly governments was simple self-defense, and the American bomb was the real threat. In 1947, when Britain could no longer afford to support the Greek government against communist rebels, President Truman asked Congress for money and announced that the United States would help any free people resisting takeover. This *containment* policy, holding communism where it was, guided American action for forty years.

The first great test came in Berlin. The city lay deep inside the Soviet zone of Germany but was itself divided into four sectors. In June 1948, angry that the Western powers were creating a separate West German state, Stalin cut every road and rail line into West Berlin. Two million people faced starvation. Rather than fight through, the United States and Britain flew in food and coal, a plane landing every few minutes for nearly a year. In May 1949 Stalin gave up and reopened the roads. The airlift had shown that the West would hold its ground without firing a shot.

By 1949 the division was fixed. Germany became two countries. In August the Soviet Union tested its own atomic bomb, years earlier than American experts had expected. In October communists won the civil war in China, the world's most populous country. Americans who had felt safe now felt surrounded. The *Cold War* was not a war in the old sense. The two sides never fought each other directly. It was a rivalry fought with money, spies, weapons, propaganda, and other people's wars, and for four decades it shaped almost everything that happened on the planet.

words.d: Churchill's phrase for the line dividing Soviet-controlled Eastern Europe from the West
the American policy of stopping communism from spreading beyond where it already held power
the rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union from about 1947 to 1991, fought without direct war
a group of countries tied together under a leading power

look.title: Truman Asks Congress to Help Greece
look.text: I believe that it must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures.
look.cite: President Harry S. Truman, address to Congress, March 12, 1947
look.prompt: Truman does not name the Soviet Union or communism. Why might he have chosen such general words, and what commitments did they open the door to?

check.q: What did Churchill mean by an iron curtain?
choices: A line dividing Soviet-controlled Eastern Europe from the West
A wall built around Berlin
A trade barrier between Britain and France
The border between Germany and Poland
check.why: In his 1946 speech Churchill described a dividing line from the Baltic to the Adriatic behind which the Soviets controlled every government.

check.q: How did the Western powers respond to the Berlin blockade of 1948?
choices: They abandoned West Berlin
They flew in food and coal for nearly a year until Stalin reopened the roads
They attacked the Soviet zone
They agreed to make Berlin part of East Germany
check.why: The airlift supplied two million people by air and showed the West would hold its ground without starting a war.

check.q: Why did Stalin see control of Eastern Europe as self-defense?
choices: The United States had invaded Poland
Eastern Europe had asked to join the Soviet Union
His country had been invaded from the west twice in thirty years
The United Nations had ordered it
check.why: After the invasions of 1914 and 1941, Stalin wanted a ring of friendly governments between the Soviet Union and Germany.

lessons.title: Marshall Plan, NATO and the Warsaw Pact
lessons.mainIdea: The United States rebuilt Western Europe with money and bound it with a military alliance, and the Soviet Union answered with its own bloc.
reading: Two years after the war, Western Europe was still broken. Cities lay in rubble, factories had no fuel, and the winter of 1947 was one of the coldest on record. Hungry, jobless people were voting for communist parties in France and Italy. In June 1947 the American Secretary of State, George Marshall, proposed that the United States pay to rebuild Europe. Over four years the *Marshall Plan* sent about thirteen billion dollars, a huge sum then, in food, machinery and raw materials to sixteen countries. The Soviet Union refused to take part and forbade its satellites to join. Western Europe's economy recovered faster than anyone had predicted.

The plan was generous and it was also strategy. Americans reasoned that prosperous people would not vote for communism, and that a rebuilt Europe would buy American goods. Both things happened. Then the Berlin blockade convinced Western leaders that they needed more than money. In April 1949 the United States, Canada and ten Western European countries signed the North Atlantic Treaty. Its key clause said that an attack on any member would be treated as an attack on all. This alliance, *NATO*, was the first peacetime military alliance the United States had ever joined. It broke with a tradition of avoiding foreign entanglements that went back to George Washington.

The Soviet Union built a mirror image. Its economic answer to the Marshall Plan tied the economies of Eastern Europe to Moscow. When West Germany joined NATO in 1955, the Soviet Union and its seven satellites signed the *Warsaw Pact*, a military alliance under Soviet command. On paper it was an alliance of equals. In practice, Soviet troops stayed in each member country, and when Hungarians rose against their government in 1956 and Czechoslovaks tried to reform theirs in 1968, Warsaw Pact tanks crushed them. NATO protested and did nothing, because doing something risked nuclear war.

Europe thus settled into two armed camps that faced each other across a line running through the middle of Germany. Behind that line, the two blocs built two different ways of life. Western Europe combined capitalism with welfare states, elections and open borders among its members. Eastern Europe had state-owned economies, one-party rule, and borders that its own citizens could not cross. The gap in wealth between the two halves grew every year, and people on the eastern side could see it on Western television. That gap, more than any army, eventually decided the contest.

words.d: the American program from 1948 to 1952 that gave about thirteen billion dollars to rebuild Western Europe
the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, a military alliance of the United States, Canada and Western Europe formed in 1949
the military alliance of the Soviet Union and its Eastern European satellites, formed in 1955
a country that is formally independent but controlled by a stronger neighbor

look.title: Generosity or Strategy?
look.text: A French factory owner in 1948 receives an American machine through the Marshall Plan and hires back forty workers. An American senator votes for the plan because he wants French voters to reject communism and buy American wheat. A Soviet newspaper calls the plan a scheme to make Europe an American colony.
look.prompt: Can an act be generous and self-interested at the same time? Which of these three views does the evidence in the reading support best?

check.q: What was the key promise in the North Atlantic Treaty?
choices: Members would share all their weapons
The United States would pay for every member's army
Members would never trade with the Soviet Union
An attack on one member would be treated as an attack on all
check.why: The collective defense clause bound the members to defend each other, a major break from earlier American practice.

check.q: Why did the Soviet Union refuse to join the Marshall Plan?
choices: It saw the plan as an American attempt to control Europe and kept its satellites out too
It did not need food
It had already recovered from the war
The United States never offered it
check.why: Moscow rejected the plan and forbade Eastern European countries to join, deepening the division of Europe.

check.q: What happened when Hungarians rose against their government in 1956?
choices: NATO sent troops to help
Warsaw Pact tanks crushed the uprising while the West protested but did not act
The United Nations took over Hungary
The Soviet Union granted Hungary independence
check.why: The West would not risk nuclear war over Hungary, so the Soviet-led intervention went unanswered.

lessons.title: Living with the Bomb
lessons.mainIdea: Both superpowers built enough nuclear weapons to destroy each other many times over, and the fear of that outcome kept them talking even as they competed.
reading: In 1952 the United States tested a hydrogen bomb hundreds of times more powerful than the one that destroyed Hiroshima. The Soviet Union tested its own the next year. In October 1957 the Soviets launched Sputnik, the first satellite, which meant a rocket could now carry a bomb across an ocean in half an hour. Americans were shaken. Both sides built missiles by the thousands, in underground silos, on bombers, and on submarines hidden under the sea. By the 1980s the two arsenals together held tens of thousands of warheads, enough to destroy every large city on Earth.

Strategists gave this situation a name that was also a description: *mutual assured destruction*, or MAD. If either side attacked, the other would still have enough weapons left to destroy the attacker. So neither side could win, and neither dared start. Some argued that the bomb had therefore prevented a third world war. Others pointed out that it had come frighteningly close to failing. Schoolchildren in Chicago and every other American city practiced hiding under their desks. Families built fallout shelters in their basements. The threat of the bomb was part of daily life.

The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962, covered in the next section, scared both sides enough to begin talking. A telephone hotline linked Washington and Moscow. In 1963 they agreed to stop testing bombs in the air. In the early 1970s President Richard Nixon and the Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev signed the first treaty limiting missile numbers, and Nixon traveled to both Moscow and, in 1972, to communist China, which had split with the Soviet Union. This easing of tension was called *détente*, a French word for relaxing. It did not end the rivalry, but it made the rivalry more predictable.

Détente faded in the late 1970s and the arms race sped up again. Then in the mid-1980s a new Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev, and President Ronald Reagan, who had called the Soviet Union an evil empire, surprised the world by becoming partners. In 1987 they signed a treaty that for the first time eliminated an entire class of nuclear missiles rather than just limiting them. Verification teams from each country inspected the other's bases. The bomb had not gone away. But the two men who controlled most of them had decided that having fewer was safer than having more.

words.d: a competition between countries to build more and better weapons than each other
the idea that a nuclear attack by either side would lead to the destruction of both, so neither dares strike
a period of eased tension between the superpowers in the 1970s, marked by treaties and visits
the explosive part of a missile or bomb

look.title: Nuclear Warheads in the World
look.cite: Federation of American Scientists estimates, rounded
look.prompt: When was the peak, and which events in the reading help explain the rise before it and the fall after it? What does the 2020 number say about whether the danger has ended?

check.q: Why did Sputnik alarm Americans in 1957?
choices: It landed in the United States
It was the first hydrogen bomb
It proved the Soviets could put a bomb on a rocket that could cross an ocean
It carried Soviet soldiers into space
check.why: A rocket able to launch a satellite could also carry a warhead to America in about half an hour.

check.q: What does mutual assured destruction mean?
choices: Both sides agreed to destroy their weapons
Both sides promised never to build hydrogen bombs
Only one side had enough weapons to win
A first strike by either side would still leave the other able to destroy the attacker, so neither dares attack
check.why: MAD describes a balance in which no attack could succeed without bringing destruction on the attacker.

check.q: What was new about the 1987 treaty between Reagan and Gorbachev?
choices: It eliminated a whole class of missiles instead of just limiting them, with inspections
It was the first treaty ever signed by the two countries
It ended the Cold War immediately
It banned all nuclear weapons in the world
check.why: Earlier treaties capped numbers; this one removed an entire category of weapons and let each side inspect the other.

sections.title: Hot Wars in a Cold War

lessons.title: China's Revolution and the Korean War
lessons.mainIdea: Communist victory in China in 1949 and the invasion of South Korea in 1950 turned the Cold War into shooting wars in Asia.
reading: China had been at war with itself, on and off, since the 1920s. On one side stood the Nationalists under Chiang Kai-shek, backed by the United States. On the other stood the communists under Mao Zedong, who built their strength among peasants in the countryside. The Japanese invasion of 1937 nearly destroyed the Nationalist armies, while the communists grew by fighting behind Japanese lines. When the civil war resumed after 1945, Mao's forces won. On October 1, 1949, he proclaimed the People's Republic of China in Beijing. Chiang fled to the island of Taiwan, which the United States protected. Two Chinas claimed to be the real one.

Mao's new state took land from landlords and gave it to peasants, then took it back into collective farms. In 1958 he launched the Great Leap Forward, ordering villages to make steel in backyard furnaces and report impossible harvests. The result was the deadliest famine of the century, with estimated deaths in the tens of millions between 1959 and 1961. In 1966 Mao unleashed the Cultural Revolution, sending bands of young Red Guards to attack teachers, officials and anyone accused of old thinking. Schools closed for years. Mao died in 1976, and his successors quietly began to undo much of what he had built.

Korea had been split at the end of World War II along the thirty-eighth parallel, Soviet troops in the north and American in the south. On June 25, 1950, North Korean forces crossed the line. Within weeks they held almost the whole peninsula. Because the Soviet delegate was boycotting the UN Security Council that month, the United States got the UN to authorize a force under General Douglas MacArthur. A daring landing at Inchon in September cut the North Korean army in half, and UN troops pushed north almost to the Chinese border. Then, in November, hundreds of thousands of Chinese soldiers poured across it.

The war seesawed back to the middle and then froze there. Fighting dragged on until an *armistice*, a stop to the fighting without a peace treaty, was signed in July 1953. The line ended up almost where it had begun. About thirty-six thousand Americans died, and Korean deaths, soldiers and civilians together, ran into the millions. Korea is still divided. The war showed the pattern of the whole Cold War: the superpowers never fought each other directly, but the countries in between paid the price. Korea also convinced Americans to keep a large army forever and to see every communist gain, anywhere, as a Soviet move.

words.d: an agreement to stop fighting that is not a full peace treaty
the Chinese party led by Chiang Kai-shek that lost the civil war and retreated to Taiwan
a line of latitude on a map; Korea was divided at the thirty-eighth
Mao's 1958 campaign to industrialize China overnight, which caused a catastrophic famine

look.title: Why the Soviet Chair Was Empty
look.text: In June 1950 the Soviet Union was boycotting the UN Security Council to protest the seating of Nationalist China instead of Mao's government. So when the United States asked the Council to authorize force in Korea, there was no Soviet delegate present to veto it.
look.prompt: What might have happened in Korea if the Soviet delegate had been in his chair? What does this tell you about how the UN could and could not act during the Cold War?

check.q: Why did Mao's communists win the Chinese civil war, according to the reading?
choices: They had American backing
They built strength among peasants and grew by fighting behind Japanese lines while the Nationalists were weakened
They controlled Taiwan
They had more nuclear weapons
check.why: The Japanese invasion nearly destroyed Nationalist armies while communist forces grew in the countryside.

check.q: How did the Korean War end?
choices: North Korea conquered the south
The United Nations conquered the north
With an armistice in 1953 that left Korea divided near where the war began
With a peace treaty uniting Korea
check.why: An armistice stopped the fighting in July 1953, but no peace treaty was signed and the country remains divided.

check.q: What happened when UN forces approached the Chinese border in November 1950?
choices: North Korea signed an armistice
China surrendered
The Soviet Union declared war on the United States
Hundreds of thousands of Chinese troops entered the war
check.why: China's massive intervention pushed UN forces back south and turned the war into a long stalemate.

lessons.title: Thirteen Days over Cuba
lessons.mainIdea: In October 1962 the discovery of Soviet missiles in Cuba brought the superpowers closer to nuclear war than at any other moment, and both leaders chose to step back.
reading: Cuba lies about ninety miles from Florida. In 1959 a young lawyer named Fidel Castro led a rebel army that overthrew a corrupt dictator friendly to the United States. Castro took over American-owned sugar mills and oil refineries, and when Washington cut off trade, he turned to the Soviet Union. In April 1961 the United States armed and landed about fourteen hundred Cuban exiles at the Bay of Pigs to overthrow him. The invasion failed within three days. Castro declared himself a communist, and the Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev saw a chance to plant weapons at America's door.

In the summer of 1962 Soviet ships secretly carried nuclear missiles to Cuba. On October 14 an American spy plane photographed the launch sites under construction. President John F. Kennedy and his advisers debated for a week in secret. The generals urged air strikes and invasion. Kennedy feared that would kill Soviet troops and start a war in Europe. On October 22 he went on television, showed the world the photographs, and announced a naval *quarantine*: American warships would stop any vessel carrying weapons to Cuba. Soviet ships kept coming. The world waited to see whether they would stop.

For the next six days nothing was certain. Soviet ships turned back from the quarantine line. But work on the missile sites continued, an American spy plane was shot down over Cuba, and American forces went to their highest alert short of war. Khrushchev sent two letters, one emotional and offering to remove the missiles if the United States promised not to invade Cuba, and a second, harder, demanding that America also remove its missiles from Turkey. Kennedy answered the first letter publicly and, through his brother Robert, secretly promised to remove the Turkish missiles later. On October 28 Khrushchev announced the missiles would go.

Decades later, records showed how close it had been. Soviet commanders in Cuba had short-range nuclear weapons and might have used them against an invasion. A Soviet submarine officer, out of contact and believing war had begun, refused to agree to fire a nuclear torpedo. Both leaders had been pushed by their own advisers to be tougher, and both had chosen a way out that let the other save face. The crisis led directly to the hotline and the test ban treaty. It also taught both sides a lesson they never forgot: in a nuclear world, an enemy needs an exit.

words.d: Kennedy's word for the naval blockade of Cuba in 1962, chosen because a blockade is an act of war
a person forced to live outside his or her own country
pushing a dangerous situation to the edge of war to force the other side to back down

look.title: Kennedy Announces the Quarantine
look.text: It shall be the policy of this Nation to regard any nuclear missile launched from Cuba against any nation in the Western Hemisphere as an attack by the Soviet Union on the United States, requiring a full retaliatory response upon the Soviet Union.
look.cite: President John F. Kennedy, televised address, October 22, 1962
look.prompt: Kennedy is telling the Soviet Union something and telling the American public something. What is each message, and why say it on television rather than in a private note?

check.q: Why did Castro turn to the Soviet Union after 1959?
choices: The United States cut off trade after he seized American-owned businesses
The Soviet Union had helped him win his revolution
Cuba had always been a Soviet ally
He wanted to invade Florida
check.why: After Castro took American sugar mills and refineries and Washington ended trade, he looked for a new partner and protector.

check.q: Why did Kennedy choose a naval quarantine instead of an air strike?
choices: The navy was the only force available
An air strike might kill Soviet troops and start a wider war, while a quarantine gave the Soviets time to back down
The missiles were not dangerous
Congress refused to allow an invasion
check.why: Kennedy wanted pressure without a first shot that could trigger war in Europe, and the quarantine left room for an exit.

check.q: What deal ended the crisis?
choices: The United States invaded Cuba
Cuba became a neutral country
Khrushchev removed the missiles in exchange for a public no-invasion pledge and a secret promise to remove American missiles from Turkey
The Soviet Union kept the missiles but promised never to use them
check.why: The public deal was a no-invasion promise; the secret part was the later removal of the Turkish missiles, which let both sides save face.

lessons.title: Vietnam and Afghanistan
lessons.mainIdea: Each superpower fought a long war against a determined local enemy, in Vietnam and in Afghanistan, and each lost, at great cost to the people whose country it was.
reading: Vietnam had been a French colony since the 1800s. On September 2, 1945, days after Japan's surrender, a nationalist and communist named Ho Chi Minh declared Vietnam independent in Hanoi, opening his speech with words borrowed from the American Declaration of Independence. France refused to let go. After eight years of war, French forces were surrounded and defeated at Dien Bien Phu in 1954. A conference at Geneva split Vietnam temporarily at the seventeenth parallel, with Ho's communists in the north and a government friendly to the West in the south, and promised elections to reunite it. The elections were never held. The United States feared Ho would win them.

American leaders believed in the *domino theory*: if Vietnam fell to communism, its neighbors would fall one after another. So they backed South Vietnam with money, advisers, and after 1965 with soldiers, more than half a million by 1969. The enemy was the North Vietnamese army and southern guerrillas called the Viet Cong, who fought from the villages and jungle, struck and vanished. American forces had the firepower to win any battle and no way to win the war. Bombing, chemical defoliants and the burning of villages turned many Vietnamese against the Americans and turned many Americans against the war. In January 1968 the communists launched the Tet Offensive, attacking cities across the south; they were beaten back, but television showed Americans a war their leaders had said was nearly won.

Protests grew, especially on college campuses. In 1968 Chicago's Democratic convention was surrounded by demonstrators and police clashes filled the news. President Nixon slowly withdrew American troops while widening the bombing, and in January 1973 signed an agreement that got the last of them out. Two years later, in April 1975, North Vietnamese tanks rolled into Saigon and the war ended with a united communist Vietnam. About fifty-eight thousand Americans had died. Vietnamese deaths, north and south, soldiers and civilians, are estimated at well over a million. The dominoes did not fall beyond Vietnam's immediate neighbors.

The Soviet Union then made a mirror-image mistake. In December 1979 it sent its army into Afghanistan to prop up a failing communist government. Afghan fighters called *mujahideen*, armed by the United States, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, fought a guerrilla war from the mountains. Soviet firepower could take any valley and hold none. After nine years and about fifteen thousand Soviet dead, along with perhaps a million Afghans, Gorbachev withdrew the last troops in February 1989. The war drained Soviet money and morale at the moment its empire was cracking. Afghanistan itself fell into civil war, with consequences that reached the United States in 2001.

words.d: the American belief that if one country became communist, its neighbors would follow one after another
a fighter who is not part of a regular army and uses surprise attacks and hiding among civilians
the Afghan fighters who resisted the Soviet occupation from 1979 to 1989
the surprise communist attacks across South Vietnam in January 1968 that shook American confidence

look.title: American Troops in Vietnam
look.cite: U.S. Department of Defense figures, rounded
look.prompt: Find the peak year. What event in the reading happened in January of that year, and how do you explain the steep fall that followed?

check.q: Why were the elections promised at Geneva in 1954 never held?
choices: Vietnam had no roads for voters
France refused to allow them
Ho Chi Minh refused to take part
The United States feared Ho Chi Minh would win
check.why: American leaders believed Ho would win a national vote, so the elections to reunite Vietnam never happened.

check.q: Why does the reading say American forces could win any battle but not the war?
choices: The enemy fought as guerrillas from villages and jungle, and the methods used to find them turned Vietnamese and Americans against the war
American soldiers were poorly trained
The North had more airplanes
The Soviet Union sent troops to Vietnam
check.why: Firepower could not defeat an enemy that struck and vanished, and bombing and burning villages cost support at home and in Vietnam.

check.q: In what way was the Soviet war in Afghanistan a mirror image of the American war in Vietnam?
choices: Both ended in a superpower victory
A superpower with overwhelming firepower could not defeat local guerrillas and withdrew after heavy losses
Both lasted only two years
Both were fought against France
check.why: In both wars a superpower propped up a weak government against guerrillas armed by its rival and finally pulled out.

lessons.title: Gandhi and the Partition of India
lessons.mainIdea: Gandhi's movement of nonviolent resistance helped end British rule in India in 1947, but independence came with a partition that killed hundreds of thousands.
reading: In 1930 a thin man of sixty in a homespun cloth walked from his home in western India toward the sea, about two hundred and forty miles, with a growing crowd behind him. When Mohandas Gandhi reached the beach at Dandi, he picked up a lump of salt. Under British law only the government could make salt, and every Indian paid a tax on it. Gandhi's act was a crime, and he meant it to be. Across India tens of thousands followed his example, and the British jailed about sixty thousand people. The Salt March showed the world a new kind of weapon, and it showed Indians that the empire could be defied.

Gandhi called his method *satyagraha*, which he translated as truth force. It meant refusing to obey unjust laws, accepting arrest and beating without striking back, and treating even the oppressor as a person who could change. It required more discipline than fighting. Gandhi trained in South Africa, where he had spent twenty years defending Indian workers against discrimination. He also believed that India must be one nation of Hindus, Muslims, Sikhs and everyone else. Many Indians disagreed with his tactics, and the Muslim League, led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah, came to demand a separate Muslim state.

World War II broke Britain's grip. Britain had used India's soldiers and money without asking, and Indian leaders were jailed for demanding independence in return. After the war Britain was bankrupt, and a new government decided to leave. The question was whether to leave one country or two. As violence between Hindus and Muslims spread in 1946 and 1947, Britain agreed to *partition*: India for the Hindu majority, Pakistan, in two pieces a thousand miles apart, for Muslims. Independence came at midnight on August 14 to 15, 1947. Gandhi refused to celebrate. He spent the day fasting for peace.

Partition set off one of the largest migrations in history. Something like fifteen million people crossed the new borders in both directions, Muslims to Pakistan and Hindus and Sikhs to India. Trains arrived full of the dead. Estimates of the killed run from several hundred thousand to over a million. In January 1948 a Hindu extremist who thought Gandhi too generous to Muslims shot him dead in Delhi. India and Pakistan have fought several wars since. Yet India became, and has remained, the world's largest democracy, and Gandhi's method traveled: Martin Luther King Jr. studied it, and civil rights marchers in Chicago and Selma used it.

words.d: Gandhi's method of nonviolent resistance, which he called truth force
dividing a country into separate states, as India and Pakistan in 1947
deliberately breaking an unjust law in public and accepting the punishment
a territory ruled by a distant country for that country's benefit

look.title: A Lump of Salt
look.text: Picture the beach at Dandi in April 1930. A crowd stands watching. Gandhi bends, scoops wet salt from the sand and holds it up. Nothing has exploded. No one has been hurt. But police reports, newspaper photographs and telegrams carry the image around the world within days.
look.prompt: Why would breaking a small law about salt shake an empire more than an attack on a police station? What did the empire lose when the world watched?

check.q: What did Gandhi mean by satyagraha?
choices: Armed revolt against British rule
A boycott of all foreign goods
Nonviolent resistance: refusing to obey unjust laws while accepting the punishment without striking back
A demand for a separate Muslim state
check.why: Truth force meant public disobedience of unjust laws with discipline and without violence, even under beating and arrest.

check.q: Why was India divided into two countries in 1947?
choices: Gandhi asked for it
Britain wanted to keep part of India
The United Nations ordered it
The Muslim League demanded a separate state and violence between communities was spreading
check.why: Jinnah's Muslim League insisted on Pakistan, and rising Hindu-Muslim violence in 1946 and 1947 led Britain to accept partition.

check.q: What was the human cost of partition described in the reading?
choices: Roughly fifteen million people crossed the new borders and hundreds of thousands or more were killed
A few thousand people moved peacefully
Only soldiers died
No one was allowed to cross the borders
check.why: Partition set off one of history's largest migrations and mass killings on both sides of the new lines.

lessons.title: Africa Wins Independence
lessons.mainIdea: Between 1957 and the mid-1970s almost every colony in Africa became independent, some by negotiation and some by war, but colonial borders and economies remained.
reading: At midnight on March 6, 1957, a crowd gathered in the capital of the British colony of the Gold Coast. The British flag came down. The flag of a new nation, Ghana, went up. Its first leader, Kwame Nkrumah, had studied in the United States. He had organized strikes and boycotts. The British had jailed him, then released him to govern. Ghana was the first colony in sub-Saharan Africa to win independence. Nkrumah told the crowd that its freedom meant nothing unless it was linked to the freedom of the whole continent. Across Africa, people listened.

The colonial powers had been weakened by World War II, and African soldiers who had fought in it came home asking why they should be ruled by strangers. The Cold War also helped: both superpowers, for their own reasons, said they opposed old-style empires. In 1960 alone, seventeen African countries became independent, most of them former French colonies. Britain let its colonies go over the next decade, usually after negotiations. Belgium abandoned the huge Congo in 1960 with almost no preparation, having trained only a handful of Congolese as doctors, officers or administrators, and the country fell into chaos within days.

Where many European settlers lived, independence came through war. In Algeria, more than a million French settlers wanted to stay French. The war from 1954 to 1962 killed hundreds of thousands of Algerians and involved torture and terror on both sides before France finally withdrew. In Kenya, Britain fought a rebellion in the 1950s and held tens of thousands of Kikuyu people in camps. Portugal clung to Angola and Mozambique until 1975. In each case, independence came, but the memory of the fighting shaped the new states.

Independence did not undo the colonial past. The new borders had been drawn in Europe in the 1880s and cut across peoples and languages, leaving nearly every state with groups that distrusted one another. Colonial economies had been built to export one or two raw materials, cocoa or copper or oil, and the price of those was set abroad. Many new leaders, including Nkrumah, became dictators, and armies overthrew governments in country after country. The superpowers backed rival sides in civil wars in Angola, Ethiopia and elsewhere. Africans had won the right to govern themselves. Whether they could build the states they wanted was a struggle that continued.

words.d: the process by which colonies became independent countries, mostly between 1945 and 1975
a person from the ruling country who moved to a colony to live and often to farm
a sudden seizure of government by a small group, often the army
an economy built to sell raw materials abroad rather than to serve its own people's needs

look.title: African Countries Becoming Independent, by Period
look.cite: Standard count of independence dates, rounded
look.prompt: Why does 1960 stand out? Using the reading, name two forces that made independence come so fast once it began.

check.q: Why was Ghana's independence in 1957 important beyond Ghana?
choices: It was the last colony in Africa
It was the first sub-Saharan colony to become independent, and Nkrumah linked its freedom to the whole continent's
It ended the Cold War
Ghana immediately conquered its neighbors
check.why: Ghana showed that independence was possible and Nkrumah made it a cause for all of Africa.

check.q: Why did the Congo fall into chaos after independence in 1960?
choices: The Soviet Union invaded it
It had no natural resources
Belgium had trained almost no Congolese to run the country and left with no preparation
Its people refused independence
check.why: Belgium's failure to prepare Congolese doctors, officers and administrators left the new state unable to function.

check.q: Why was independence in Algeria and Kenya won by war rather than negotiation?
choices: The United Nations refused to help
Their leaders rejected nonviolence
Both were French colonies
Large populations of European settlers wanted to keep colonial rule
check.why: Where many settlers lived, the ruling country fought to keep the colony, and independence took years of violence.

lessons.title: The Middle East after 1948
lessons.mainIdea: The creation of Israel in 1948, the Palestinian refugees it produced, oil, and superpower rivalry made the Middle East one of the Cold War's most dangerous regions.
reading: After World War I Britain had governed Palestine under a League of Nations mandate, and had promised, in 1917, to support a national home there for Jewish people while protecting the rights of the Arabs who lived there. Jewish immigration grew, especially as Nazi persecution spread, and Arab and Jewish communities clashed. After the Holocaust, pressure for a Jewish state became overwhelming. In November 1947 the United Nations voted to divide Palestine into a Jewish state and an Arab state. Jewish leaders accepted the plan. Arab leaders rejected it, and fighting began at once.

On May 14, 1948, David Ben-Gurion proclaimed the State of Israel. The next day the armies of neighboring Arab countries attacked. Israel won, and by the armistice of 1949 it held more land than the UN plan had given it. During the war, roughly seven hundred thousand Palestinian Arabs fled or were driven from their homes and were not allowed to return. They and their descendants, now numbering in the millions, are the Palestinian *refugees* whose situation remains unresolved. Israelis call 1948 the War of Independence. Palestinians call it the Nakba, the catastrophe. Both names describe real events.

The conflict became part of the Cold War. The Soviet Union armed Egypt and Syria; the United States became Israel's main supporter. In June 1967 Israel, striking first against Egyptian forces massing on its border, defeated Egypt, Syria and Jordan in six days and occupied the West Bank, Gaza, the Sinai and the Golan Heights, placing about a million more Palestinians under its rule. In October 1973 Egypt and Syria attacked on the Jewish holy day of Yom Kippur; Israel recovered, but only after heavy losses and an American airlift. Arab oil states then cut production and stopped shipments to the United States. Gasoline prices in Illinois and everywhere else jumped, and lines formed at the pumps.

The *oil embargo* taught the world that the region's oil was a weapon, and it made the Persian Gulf a vital interest for both superpowers. In 1978 President Jimmy Carter brought the leaders of Egypt and Israel to Camp David, and Egypt became the first Arab state to make peace with Israel. Then in 1979 a revolution in Iran overthrew a pro-American king and created an Islamic republic hostile to both superpowers. Radicals held fifty-two Americans hostage for over a year. The Middle East would keep proving that the Cold War's two-sided map could not explain everything.

words.d: a person forced to flee his or her home and country because of war, persecution or disaster
the 1973 decision by Arab oil producers to stop selling oil to the United States and cut production
the control of a territory by a foreign military force
Arabic for catastrophe; the Palestinian name for the flight and expulsion of 1948

look.title: One Year, Two Names
look.text: A grandmother in Tel Aviv remembers May 1948 as the month her people, three years after the death camps, finally had a state and an army to protect them. A grandmother in a camp near Beirut remembers the same month as the one when her family locked the door of their house in Jaffa, took the key, and never went back.
look.prompt: Both memories are true. Why does the same event carry opposite names for different peoples? What does a historian owe to each of these women?

check.q: What did the United Nations decide about Palestine in November 1947?
choices: To divide it into a Jewish state and an Arab state
To keep it under British rule
To make it part of Egypt
To make it a single Arab state
check.why: The UN partition plan proposed two states; Jewish leaders accepted it and Arab leaders rejected it.

check.q: What happened to about seven hundred thousand Palestinian Arabs in 1948?
choices: They became citizens of Israel
They fled or were driven from their homes and were not allowed to return
They moved to Europe
They were given land in Egypt
check.why: The refugees of 1948 and their descendants remain a central unresolved issue of the conflict.

check.q: How did the 1973 war reach ordinary Americans?
choices: American troops were sent to Egypt
The Soviet Union attacked American ships
Arab oil producers cut off oil shipments, and gasoline prices jumped with lines at the pumps
The United States made peace with Iran
check.why: The oil embargo that followed the war showed Americans how much they depended on Middle Eastern oil.

lessons.title: Apartheid and Its End
lessons.mainIdea: South Africa built a legal system of racial separation in 1948 and dismantled it in 1994 after decades of resistance, world pressure, and a negotiated transfer of power.
reading: In 1948 the National Party won an election in South Africa in which only white people could vote, and it made *apartheid*, an Afrikaans word for apartness, the law of the land. Every person was classified by race. Black South Africans, about three-quarters of the population, were assigned to scattered homelands that made up about thirteen percent of the country's land. They needed passes to enter white cities, where they worked in mines and kitchens but could not live. Marriage across race lines was a crime. Beaches, buses, schools and hospitals were separate and grossly unequal. It was a system for keeping cheap labor and total power in white hands.

Resistance was led by the African National Congress, or ANC, which for years followed Gandhi's methods of nonviolent protest. In March 1960 police at Sharpeville opened fire on a crowd protesting the pass laws and killed sixty-nine people, most shot in the back. The government banned the ANC. One of its young leaders, a lawyer named Nelson Mandela, concluded that nonviolence alone would not work and helped form an armed wing that sabotaged power lines and government buildings. He was captured, and in 1964 he was sentenced to life in prison. He spent twenty-seven years there, much of it breaking rocks on Robben Island.

Inside South Africa, protest never stopped. In 1976 schoolchildren in the township of Soweto marched against being taught in Afrikaans, and police killed hundreds in the months that followed. Outside, the world slowly turned against apartheid. Athletes were banned from international sports. Students in the United States, including at Illinois campuses, demanded that their universities sell shares in companies doing business in South Africa. In 1986 Congress passed economic sanctions over President Reagan's veto. The Cold War had given South Africa's government cover, since it called every opponent a communist. As the Cold War ended, the cover disappeared.

In February 1990 the new president, F. W. de Klerk, released Mandela and legalized the ANC. Four years of hard negotiation followed, while violence between rival groups killed thousands. Mandela insisted that the goal was not revenge but a country that belonged to everyone. In April 1994 South Africans of every race lined up, some for hours, in the first election in which all adults could vote. Mandela became president. A commission then heard testimony from victims and perpetrators of apartheid crimes, offering amnesty for full confession. Apartheid's legal structure was gone. Its economic legacy, and the argument over how to repair it, remains.

words.d: South Africa's legal system of racial separation and white rule from 1948 to 1994
penalties such as trade bans used by countries to pressure another government to change
a segregated area outside a South African city where Black people were forced to live
an official pardon for past offenses, often in exchange for telling the truth about them

look.title: Mandela in the Dock
look.text: At his trial in 1964, Mandela told the court that he had fought against white domination and against Black domination alike, and that he held the ideal of a free society in which all people lived together in harmony with equal opportunities. He said it was an ideal he hoped to live for and achieve, but if need be, one for which he was prepared to die.
look.cite: Nelson Mandela, statement at the Rivonia Trial, April 1964 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Mandela spoke of a society free from domination by any race, not just an end to white rule. Why might that choice of words have mattered thirty years later when he negotiated with the government?

check.q: What was the purpose of the pass laws under apartheid?
choices: To let Black South Africans vote
To separate Afrikaans speakers from English speakers
To give everyone identity cards for travel abroad
To control where Black South Africans could go and keep them out of white cities except as workers
check.why: Passes controlled the movement of Black South Africans, who could work in white cities but not live there.

check.q: Why did the ANC turn from nonviolence to sabotage after 1960?
choices: After police killed sixty-nine protesters at Sharpeville and the ANC was banned, leaders like Mandela concluded nonviolence alone would not work
The Soviet Union ordered it
The United States promised weapons
Gandhi told them to
check.why: Sharpeville and the ban convinced Mandela and others that peaceful protest by itself could not end apartheid.

check.q: How did the end of the Cold War help end apartheid?
choices: The Soviet Union invaded South Africa
It removed the government's excuse that all opponents were communists
The United States stopped caring about Africa
It caused Mandela's arrest
check.why: South Africa's government had used anti-communism to win Western tolerance; when the Cold War ended, that cover was gone.

lessons.title: 1989: The Year of Revolutions
lessons.mainIdea: In a single year, peaceful movements across Eastern Europe toppled communist governments because the Soviet Union, under Gorbachev, would no longer send tanks.
reading: Mikhail Gorbachev became leader of the Soviet Union in 1985 and found a country that was losing. Its factories made shoddy goods. Its farms could not feed the country without buying American grain. Its war in Afghanistan was a disaster. The arms race with a richer America was bankrupting it. Gorbachev announced two policies. *Glasnost*, meaning openness, let newspapers and citizens criticize the government for the first time in sixty years. *Perestroika*, meaning restructuring, loosened state control of the economy. He also told the leaders of Eastern Europe that the Soviet army would no longer save them from their own people.

Poland moved first. Its independent trade union, Solidarity, had been founded in the Gdansk shipyard in 1980 by an electrician named Lech Walesa and had survived years of being banned. In 1989 the government, unable to fix the economy, agreed to talks and then to partly free elections in June. Solidarity won almost every seat it was allowed to contest. By late summer Poland had a non-communist prime minister and no tanks had moved. Hungary, watching, dismantled the barbed wire on its border with Austria in May and opened it fully in September. The hole in the iron curtain let East Germans out, and that led to the events in Berlin described at the start of this chapter.

After the wall opened on November 9, the rest came in weeks. In Czechoslovakia, huge crowds in Prague filled the squares night after night, jingling their keys, and by the end of December the playwright Václav Havel, jailed by the communists months earlier, was president. Bulgaria's leader was pushed out. Only in Romania was there blood: the dictator Nicolae Ceausescu ordered troops to fire on protesters, the army turned against him, and he was executed on Christmas Day. In one year, six governments that had seemed permanent were gone, almost all without a shot fired.

Not every communist government fell. In China, students had filled Beijing's Tiananmen Square in the spring of 1989 demanding reform, and on the night of June 3 to 4 the army cleared the square with tanks and gunfire, killing hundreds or more. China's rulers kept power by choosing force. Eastern Europe's rulers, without Soviet backing and unwilling to order a massacre, did not. Historians point to many causes for 1989: economic failure, Gorbachev's choices, Western pressure, the pope's support for Poland, television. But the sequence of the year shows one thing clearly. Once people stopped being afraid, the system had nothing else to hold it up.

words.d: Gorbachev's policy of openness, allowing criticism and free discussion in the Soviet Union
Gorbachev's policy of restructuring the Soviet economy with less state control
the independent Polish trade union, founded in 1980, that led the peaceful end of communist rule in Poland
a person who openly opposes a government that does not allow opposition

look.title: The Domino Year
look.text: June 1989: Poland votes. September: Hungary opens its border. November 9: the Berlin Wall opens. November 17 to December 29: Czechoslovakia's Velvet Revolution. December 25: Romania's dictator falls. June 4, the same year: tanks clear Tiananmen Square in Beijing.
look.prompt: Americans had feared dominoes falling toward communism. In 1989 they fell the other way. What was the same in each Eastern European case, and what was different about China?

check.q: What was the most important thing Gorbachev told Eastern European leaders?
choices: That they should join NATO
That they must hold free elections immediately
That the Soviet army would no longer save them from their own people
That the Berlin Wall must come down
check.why: Without the threat of Soviet tanks, governments that had ruled by fear had to face their citizens alone.

check.q: How did Hungary's decision in 1989 lead to the fall of the Berlin Wall?
choices: Hungary invaded East Germany
Hungary asked the UN to remove the wall
Hungary joined West Germany
Opening its border with Austria let East Germans escape west, which pressured East Germany to ease travel rules
check.why: The hole in the iron curtain drained East Germany of people and forced its government into the decision that ended the wall.

check.q: What was different about China in 1989?
choices: China's rulers chose force and cleared Tiananmen Square with tanks, keeping power
China's protesters demanded a return to Mao
China had no protests
China joined the Warsaw Pact
check.why: Unlike Eastern European leaders, China's government was willing to order a massacre, and it survived.

lessons.title: The Soviet Union Dissolves
lessons.mainIdea: Reforms meant to save the Soviet Union instead released the forces that broke it apart, and on Christmas Day 1991 it ceased to exist.
reading: Gorbachev's openness had a result he did not intend. The Soviet Union was made of fifteen republics, Russia by far the largest, and once people could speak freely, many said they wanted out. The three Baltic republics of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, seized by Stalin in 1940, formed a human chain of about two million people across all three countries in August 1989 to demand independence. Georgians, Armenians, Ukrainians and others followed. Meanwhile the half-reformed economy produced shortages worse than before. Shelves in Moscow stood empty. Gorbachev was praised abroad and increasingly hated at home.

In August 1991 a group of hard-line generals and party officials tried to stop the breakup. They placed Gorbachev under house arrest at his vacation home and sent tanks into Moscow. Boris Yeltsin, the elected president of the Russian republic, climbed onto one of those tanks outside the Russian parliament and called on the people to resist. Crowds surrounded the building. Soldiers refused to fire. Within three days the *coup* had collapsed. Gorbachev returned to Moscow, but power had passed to Yeltsin, who banned the Communist Party in Russia.

The republics now left one after another. Ukraine voted for independence in December by more than ninety percent. On December 8 the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus met and declared that the Soviet Union no longer existed. On December 25, 1991, Gorbachev resigned, and that evening the red flag over the Kremlin was lowered for the last time and the Russian flag raised. Seventy-four years after Lenin's revolution, the state it had created was gone. The Cold War was over, and no shot had been fired between the superpowers.

The end raised questions the world is still answering. Fifteen new countries appeared, several with nuclear weapons on their soil, which were eventually moved to Russia. Russia's economy collapsed in the 1990s and its people's savings vanished, leaving bitterness that later leaders would use. Some Americans concluded that their side had won and that history had settled the question of how to govern. Others noted that the Soviet Union fell mainly from inside. The next chapter picks up in the world that this ending made: one superpower, dozens of new states, and an economy, and a set of problems, that no single country could contain.

words.d: here, one of the fifteen units of the Soviet Union, such as Russia, Ukraine or Estonia
a sudden, illegal attempt to seize control of a government
a person who opposes reform and wants to keep the old system by force if necessary

look.title: A Challenge at the Wall
look.text: General Secretary Gorbachev, if you seek peace, if you seek prosperity for the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, if you seek liberalization: Come here to this gate! Mr. Gorbachev, open this gate! Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!
look.cite: President Ronald Reagan, speech at the Brandenburg Gate, West Berlin, June 12, 1987
look.prompt: Reagan spoke these words two years before the wall fell. Based on this chapter, how much credit should a speech get, compared with the people of Leipzig or the guards at Bornholmer Street?

check.q: What unexpected result did glasnost have inside the Soviet Union?
choices: The economy immediately improved
Once people could speak freely, many republics demanded independence
The Communist Party became more popular
The arms race ended
check.why: Openness let Balts, Ukrainians, Georgians and others say they wanted out, which the old system had never allowed.

check.q: How did the August 1991 coup end?
choices: The generals took power for a decade
Gorbachev fled to the West
Crowds resisted, soldiers refused to fire, and the coup collapsed in three days, leaving Yeltsin the strongest figure
NATO troops entered Moscow
check.why: Yeltsin's stand on the tank and the soldiers' refusal to shoot broke the coup and shifted power away from Gorbachev.

check.q: Which statement best matches the reading's view of why the Soviet Union ended?
choices: It was defeated in battle by the United States
It was destroyed by a nuclear accident
It voted to join NATO
It fell mainly from inside, as reforms released forces that broke it apart
check.why: The reading stresses internal causes: economic failure, national independence movements, and a failed coup, with no shot fired between superpowers.

review.q: Which American policy is best described as holding communism where it already was?
choices: Containment
Appeasement
Détente
Isolation
review.why: Containment, announced by Truman in 1947, aimed to stop the spread of communism without directly attacking the Soviet Union.

review.q: What did the Marshall Plan and NATO have in common?
choices: Both were Soviet programs
Both were American efforts to strengthen Western Europe against communism, one with money and one with a military alliance
Both were created by the United Nations
Both ended in 1949
review.why: The Marshall Plan rebuilt Western economies and NATO bound the West militarily; together they fixed the division of Europe.

review.q: What pattern did the Korean War set for the rest of the Cold War?
choices: The superpowers fought each other directly
The United Nations always stayed neutral
Wars were fought in countries between the superpowers, which never fought each other directly
China and the Soviet Union always fought on opposite sides
review.why: Korea showed the superpowers backing opposite sides while a third country paid the price.

review.q: What lesson did both leaders take from the Cuban Missile Crisis?
choices: That treaties are useless
That air strikes always work
That Cuba should be invaded
That an enemy in a nuclear world needs a way out
review.why: Kennedy and Khrushchev each chose an exit that let the other save face, and the crisis led to the hotline and the test ban.

review.q: Why did the United States lose in Vietnam and the Soviet Union lose in Afghanistan?
choices: Both faced local guerrillas who could not be beaten by firepower alone, while support at home collapsed
Both were defeated by the other superpower's army
Both ran out of weapons
Both were expelled by the United Nations
review.why: In both wars overwhelming firepower could win battles but not defeat a guerrilla enemy rooted in the population.

review.q: What did Gandhi's Salt March and the ANC's early campaigns have in common?
choices: Both used armed attacks on soldiers
Both used nonviolent disobedience of unjust laws
Both demanded partition
Both were organized by the United States
review.why: The ANC followed Gandhi's methods for years before turning to sabotage after the Sharpeville massacre.

review.q: Which problem did most new African states face after independence?
choices: Too many trained administrators
Immediate membership in NATO
Borders drawn in Europe that cut across peoples, and economies built to export one or two raw materials
A lack of any natural resources
review.why: Colonial borders and export economies remained after the flags changed, shaping conflicts and poverty.

review.q: What single change made the peaceful revolutions of 1989 possible?
choices: A decision by the United Nations
A NATO invasion
China's support for reform
Gorbachev's refusal to use the Soviet army to keep Eastern European governments in power
review.why: Once governments could not count on Soviet tanks and would not order massacres, their citizens no longer feared them.
